messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 24
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Pharmacist
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 58

At 24, he is one of the youngest pharmacists in the hospital dispensary, known by coworkers as careful, soft-spoken, and almost impossibly precise. He double-checks decimal points, catches interactions others miss, and keeps his bench immaculate. From the outside, he seems composed. But when he talks about the last two years, his story always begins with his younger sister.

He grows up in a close Oceanian family where cousins move in and out of one another’s houses and no one eats alone unless they want to. His sister is two years younger, loud where he is quiet, impulsive where he is cautious. She calls him when she needs help with university forms, with rent, with life. He likes being the dependable one. Even after he moves for pharmacy school, they speak most days, often late at night when she is walking home or upset about a boyfriend or asking what to take for a fever.

The traumatic night begins ordinarily. He is finishing a shift placement and is too tired to answer her first call. She leaves a voice message, half laughing, saying she is at a party and her ex is there, “being weird,” but she will sort it out. He texts that he will call after his shower. Before he does, their cousin rings him instead, panicked and crying. There has been an assault in a parking lot outside the party. His sister has been found badly injured.

He remembers almost nothing of the drive to the emergency department except red lights he does not believe apply to him. In the trauma bay he catches fragments—the snap of gloves, blood on concrete-colored skin, a nurse asking for space, his sister’s face swollen almost beyond recognition. He hears someone say her name and does not understand for a moment that they mean this person on the bed. He feels sick with the thought that she called and he did not pick up. For days after, he stays in the hospital waiting room in the same clothes, sleeping sitting up, drinking coffee that tastes burnt and metallic. He speaks to surgeons and social workers and police officers, but later cannot recall their words in order. His sister survives, though with fractures, internal injuries, and a long rehabilitation that leaves her frightened, easily startled, and unwilling to be alone.

In the months that follow, he tells himself he should be grateful she is alive. Other people say this too. He returns to pharmacy training, but life no longer moves in a straight line. At work, the antiseptic smell on the wards throws him back to that first night. The shrill tone of a monitor can make his chest seize before he remembers where he is. When an agitated man raises his voice at the prescription counter, his whole body tightens and he has to fight the urge to get behind a locked door. He starts scanning every room automatically, noting exits, large men, people who seem intoxicated. He tells himself this is sensible, not fear.

Sleep becomes the place he dreads most. He dreams not only of what he saw but of what he imagines happened before anyone found her. In some dreams her missed call keeps flashing while he stands frozen. He wakes sweating, heart pounding, already ashamed. He begins staying up late with streaming shows or pharmacy revision videos so he will fall asleep from exhaustion. In the morning he feels dull and brittle. Small mistakes haunt him; if he mislabels a shelf or nearly hands over the wrong strength before catching himself, he is flooded with panic and self-disgust. He checks and rechecks everything, then worries his caution looks strange.

Outside work, his world narrows. He avoids parties, crowded bars, parking structures, and any conversation about violence against women. Family gatherings become complicated because his sister’s pain sits in the room even when no one names it. If she is quiet, he watches her. If she goes to the bathroom and does not return quickly, he feels a rush of alarm. She notices and tells him to stop looking at her like she might disappear. He feels guilty for hovering and guilty when he tries to step back. He has stopped dating altogether; he cannot tolerate the thought of being responsible for someone’s safety and failing again.

What troubles him most is that his mind does not behave as he believes it should. He knows, professionally and intellectually, that he did not cause the assault. He can explain trauma responses to patients collecting antidepressants or sleeping tablets, can speak calmly about adherence and side effects. But when he sees his sister hesitate before getting out of a car at night, or hears her lock the door twice, the old certainty returns: he should have answered, should have gone, should have prevented all of it. He carries that belief like a private ritual of punishment.

Now, even on good days, he lives as if catastrophe is always one distracted moment away. He keeps his phone volume on high through every shift. He startles when it rings and cannot ignore it. He says he is tired all the time, but underneath the tiredness is something more constant—a sense that the world has already proved itself capable of tearing through the people he loves, and that no amount of knowledge, competence, or vigilance has been enough to stop it.
